**ECB selects 36 payment providers for digital euro pilot phase**

*The selection of participants, from major processors to fintechs, sets the shape of the digital euro's commercial ecosystem ahead of a pilot starting in late 2027.*

The European Central Bank has chosen 36 payment service providers to take part in the digital euro pilot, scheduled to begin in the second half of 2027 and run for 12 months. The cohort spans incumbent processors such as Nexi alongside fintechs such as Stripe, SumUp and Revolut, signalling the ECB's intent to test the digital euro across a broad cross-section of the payments market rather than confining it to traditional banking channels.

The selection follows the European Parliament's vote in July to advance the digital euro regulation to final trilogue negotiations. With legislative and technical workstreams now running in parallel, the pilot will serve as the practical proving ground for distribution models, merchant acceptance and consumer experience. The inclusion of non-bank providers is consistent with the ECB's stated position that the digital euro should complement private payment solutions, though the trade body representing open banking providers has warned separately that the current legislative text could restrict their participation in the live scheme.

For payments strategists, the participant list is the clearest signal yet of which firms the ECB considers credible distribution partners and where commercial opportunities may sit when the digital euro moves toward production.

*Sources: [ECB selects 36 payment service providers to join digital euro pilot](https://www.ecb.europa.eu//press/pr/date/2026/html/ecb.pr260714~8cd07d9d45.en.html) — ECB | [ECB selects 36 PSPs for digital euro pilot phase](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48084/ecb-selects-36-psps-for-digital-euro-pilot-phase?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra | [Nexi to participate in the digital euro pilot phase](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110408/nexi-to-participate-in-the-digital-euro-pilot-phase?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra | [Stripe, SumUp and Revolut among firms chosen to test 'digital euro'](https://www.independent.ie/business/stripe-sumup-and-revolut-among-firms-chosen-to-test-digital-euro/a/158690988.html) — Irish Independent*

**UK government opens consultation on modernising payments regulation**

*The consultation covers tokenised payments, open banking governance and the broader regulatory framework, marking the start of a formal overhaul of UK payment services rules.*

The UK government has launched a public consultation on modernising its payment services regulatory framework, addressing how rules should adapt to account for tokenised payments, open banking and evolving market structures. The consultation follows Rachel Reeves's announcement last week of an open finance push focused on SME lending and sits alongside the separate infrastructure consultation launched in late June.

Where the June consultation focused on next-generation retail payment infrastructure, this exercise targets the regulatory architecture itself — the rules governing authorisation, conduct and supervision of payment firms. The scope explicitly includes how open banking governance should evolve and how the framework should accommodate token-based payment instruments, areas where the UK's post-Brexit regulatory flexibility gives it room to diverge from the EU's PSD3 approach.

The timing places two major consultations — on infrastructure and regulation — in the market simultaneously, requiring industry participants to engage on both the plumbing and the rules in parallel. Responses will shape the UK's competitive positioning relative to the EU's own payments modernisation programme.

*Sources: [UK Government Open Consultation: Modernising Payment Services Regulation](https://mondovisione.com/media-and-resources/news/uk-government-open-consultation-modernising-payment-services-regulation-2026714/) — Mondovisione*

**US fintechs say CFPB open banking fee proposal violates Trump executive order**

*The industry pushback escalates the dispute over the rewritten Section 1033 rule, with fintechs arguing that allowing banks to charge data-sharing fees contradicts the administration's own deregulatory mandate.*

US fintech firms are challenging the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's revised open banking rule, arguing that its provision allowing banks to charge fees for customer data sharing violates a Trump executive order aimed at reducing regulatory burdens. The CFPB rewrote its Section 1033 rule in June, narrowing the scope of data covered and introducing a fee mechanism that the original rule had prohibited.

The industry response frames the fee provision not just as bad policy but as legally inconsistent with the administration's own directives. The CFPB had positioned the rewrite as aligning the rule with the administration's deregulatory agenda, but fintechs contend that enabling banks to monetise data access creates a new barrier rather than removing one. The National Association of Convenience Stores has separately urged adoption of the open banking rule, arguing it protects consumers' existing legal right to share their own financial data.

The dispute matters beyond the US because the question of who bears the cost of data sharing — and whether incumbents can charge for API access — is live in every open banking jurisdiction. The EU's PSD3 framework and the UK's evolving model are both navigating the same tension, and the US outcome will influence how other regulators approach it.

*Sources: [CFPB Data-Rationing Proposal Violates Trump Order, Fintechs Say](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/banking-law/cfpb-data-rationing-proposal-violates-trump-order-fintechs-say) — Bloomberg Law News | [NACS Urges Adoption of Open Banking Rule](https://www.convenience.org/stay-current/news/2026/july/14/nacs-urges-adoption-of-open-banking-rule) — Convenience*

**GoCardless integrates pay-by-bank into Sage for small business accounting**

*The partnership embeds open banking payments directly into accounting software used by millions of small businesses, testing whether pay-by-bank can displace cards and direct debits in routine B2B transactions.*

GoCardless is expanding its partnership with Sage to integrate its Pay by Bank feature directly within Sage Business Cloud Accounting. The integration allows small businesses to offer open banking payments as a checkout option alongside existing methods, embedding account-to-account payments into the invoicing workflow rather than requiring a separate payment step.

The move is notable for where it positions pay-by-bank: not as a consumer checkout alternative competing with cards at e-commerce scale, but as a B2B payment method integrated into the accounting tools that small businesses already use daily. Sage's installed base across UK and European SMEs gives the integration immediate distribution, and the combination of payment initiation with accounting reconciliation addresses one of the persistent friction points in small business payments.

GoCardless reported its first profitable quarter earlier this year as payment volumes doubled. Embedding pay-by-bank into established software platforms, rather than competing for placement at consumer checkout, represents a distinct distribution strategy that sidesteps many of the conversion challenges that have slowed pay-by-bank adoption in retail settings.

*Sources: [Sage, GoCardless add Pay by Bank for small businesses](https://thepaypers.com/payments/news/sage-gocardless-add-pay-by-bank-for-small-businesses) — The Paypers | [How Open Banking Feature From GoCardless and Sage Aids SMBs](https://fintechmagazine.com/news/gocardless-sage-alliance-helps-smbs-with-open-banking) — FinTech Magazine | [GoCardless expands partnership with Sage to integrate Pay by Bank for small businesses](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/gocardless-expands-partnership-with-sage-to-integrate-pay-by-bank-for-small-businesses/) — Openbankingexpo*
